george-hopkins-monticello-1885-08.A4:
KILLED IN HIS CELL.
Monticello Vigilants Shoot a Black Desperado Through the Bars.
INDIAN SPRINGS July 31. One of the
Monticello Vigilants Shoot a Black Desperado Through the Bars.

INDIAN SPRINGS, July 31.—One of the most cold-blooded and diabolical murders ever committed in the State occurred at Monticello on Wednesday night. Some four weeks ago a young man in Jasper county had an altercation with a negro by the name of John Hopkins, in which the former was severely cut. The negro was arrested in McDonough Tuesday, and placed in the Monticello jail for safe keeping. The jail is supplied with an iron cage with two small openings to admit air and light. Into this cage the negro was placed.

Wednesday night unknown parties visited the jail. Some kindled a fire on one side of the jail, while one of the party on the opposite side placed the muzzle of a gun, which was charged heavily with buckshot, within a foot of the sleeping negro's head, who could be seen by the light from the fire. He then aroused the man, calling him by name, and as he attempted to arise the gun was discharged, tearing away a portion of his head and breaking his neck.

There is no clue to the perpetrators, but no effort will be spared to ferret them out and bring them to justice. While the negro was a bad character, the act is greatly deplored by all law-abiding citizens.

Killed by Masked Men.
NICHOLLE Co Aug 1 A vole
Monticello, Ga., Aug 1.—A volley of shots, apparently from half a dozen guns, aroused the people of this town early yesterday morning. Those who were out first saw four masked men running in different directions. In the jail the dead body of Jack Hopkins was found, shot to pieces with buckshot. Several days ago Hopkins quarreled with his employer, George Gilmore, a wealthy planter of this county. While Gilmore was attending to his stock, he was struck on the back of the head and fell insensible to the ground, when Hopkins set upon him with a knife. He was interrupted in this fiendish work by half a dozen men, whom Hopkins successfully resisted, cutting his way through them with his bloody knife and escaping to the woods. A posse of men with dogs started in pursuit, keeping on the trail until Tuesday morning, when they overtook him in McDonough and arrested him. He was more like a wild animal than a man. On the way back he was tied hand and foot, so determined was he in attaching his guards. In the jail there is one of Pauley's patented cells. Into this Hopkins was placed and left for the night. About twenty masked men rode quietly up to the edge of the town at 11 o'clock Thursday night. Four of them were detailed to proceed to the jail, armed with double-barreled shotguns. As they approached the cell, which has openings for ventilation, the imprisoned wretch begged for mercy. The four men, however, placed the muzzles of their guns at the openings and fired, fairly filling the prisoner with shot. Quickly reloading, they discharged their guns again and, turning upon their heels, regained their companions and rode away.
george-hopkins-monticello-1885-08.A6:
LYNCHED FOR A LIGHT OFFENCE.
MONTICELLO, Ga., Aug. 1 (Special). Between 12 and 1 o'clock yesterday morning a gang of masked men rode into town and proceeded to the jail, where George Hopkins was confined in one of Pauloy's patent cells. Placing the muzzles of their guns between the bars they discharged load after load of backshot into the prisoner, who pleaded piteously for his life. The jailer did not learn of the tragedy until he brought breakfast to the dead man. Hopkins had severely wounded his employer, one Glimore, a few days before.

LYNCHINGS IN GEORGIA.—Two sensational lynchings have recently occurred in Georgia. On the night of the 28th ultimo, Thomas Brantley, a white man was taken from Bainbridge jail and hanged. His offence, which so infuriated the quiet farmers of the Southwest part of the State was barbarous cruelty to his wife. Since his wedding, eighteen months ago, he subjected his wife to the most brutal treatment. She was the widow of Dr. James O'Neal, a member of a rich and highly respectable family. She was beaten almost daily. Her slightest act was taken by him as a provocation for his diabolical treatment. A few months ago he compelled her to witness and even assist him while assaulting a negro servant. Recently his treatment grew worse. Last week he was enraged because she accepted a piece of wartermelon from a gentleman at a picnic. On the way home he beat her repeatedly with a carriage whip and so savagely that her back and neck were raw and covered with blood. At home he knocked her down, broke two of her ribs, and poured a vial of turpentine over her naked body and wounds. The pain nearly drove her into insanity. Until then she had kept her husband's inhuman actions secret. Suffering horrible torture, she escaped from bed and hurried to her brother's home. The next day Brantley was arrested. As the story of her suffering spread excitement and indignation grew. Sixty men attacked the jail, overpowered the Sheriff and aids, tore away the cell door, and carried the wretch out. He seemed to expect lynching, and implored the other prisoners not to tell the mob where he was confined. They refused, and directed the masked men where to find Brantley. He shrieked "Murder" and begged for mercy, but his captors were relentless. After swinging him by a plough line to a limb his body was riddled with bullets. He came to Georgia from Alabama a few years ago, and by an attractive manner won the respect of the people with whom he came in contact. Public sentiment approves his death.

Placing the muzzles of their guns to the openings they discharged hundreds of buckshot into the wretch, who was pleading for his life. Strange to say, the jailor did not learn of the tragedy until he brought breakfast to the dead man. Hopkins had severely wounded his employer, Gillmore, a few days before.

A detective officer of Macon has been engaged for some weeks in a search for a supposed insurance swindler. Some time ago a man insured his life for several thousand dollars, and soon after it was reported that he had been killed. The peculiar circumstances surrounding the alleged killing, among them being the fact that the body could not be found, led the officers of the company to believe that an attempt was being made to swindle them. The man in question married in Macon, and it is said that his wife, now in Atlanta, has been shadowed by a detective for more than a month. A detective has been to New York, to Texas, and to other parts of the country searching for the supposed swindler, but has not been able to discover anything of consequence.

Lumpkin Independent: While Master Walter Gillis was trying to throw his shepherd dog, Grover Cleveland, into Grimes' pond, holding the dog by his rear legs, Walter slipped into the pond himself. Grover clung to the bank with his fore feet, while Walter held on to the hand feet, and felt for the bottom in vain with his own feet. Grover looked anxiously over his shoulder at his young master, as if he would like to rescue him from the water, but his strength was not sufficient to pull both himself and Walter out. He held to the bank, however, and kept Walter's head out of the water until some boys pulled him out. Walter took a long look at the dog and said: "Grover, when I get you home I'll give you more candy and crackers than you ever had before in your life."

At Monticello, Tuesday, the Coroner's jury met to investigate further the killing of John Hopkins, colored. They examined twenty or thirty witnesses, but could get no proof sufficient to authorize them to issue a warrant for any one's arrest. The jury rendered the following verdict: "We, the jury, find that Jack Hopkins, colored, came to his death by a shot from a double-barreled shotgun in the hands of some unknown parties, and recommend that the Governor and the County Commissioners offer a sufficient reward to bring the guilty parties to justice." It is reported that Hopkins' wife is going to swear out a warrant against Mr. Gilmore, charging him with the killing. It is also rumored that she is going to sue the county for damages. Up to this writing no warrant has been issued.

At Oglethorpe Tuesday Squire Bryan was brought before Ordinary C. A. Greer on a writ of lunacy and was declared a lunatic. Squire has a history. Five years ago he was indicted by the grand jury of Taylor county for an assault with intent to murder, in trying to cut his wife's throat. He was convicted and sentenced to 10 years in the penitentiary. After his sentence he was taken back to jail, and while there he got possession of a pocketknife and deliberately cut his eyes out of his head. This remarkable act, however, did not keep the law from being enforced, to some extent at least. He was taken to the coal mines, and was worsened two years, when he was pardoned out by Gov. Colquitt. Since then he has been gradually losing his mind, and was Tuesday declared a fit subject for the asylum.

Dr. Joseph Jones, of Norcross, makes the following statement in refutation of the facts by the New York Tribune: "Gen. Bethune began exhibiting Blind Tom when he was about 10 years of age, and when he was a slave, as he had a right to do. After he was made free, Bethune entered into a contract with Mingo, his former slave and Tom's father, agreeing to pay him $500 per annum for Tom's services. He placed Mingo and his family in a comfortable house, the old homestead of the Bethunes, near Columbus, Ga., and paid the $500 promptly. After the expiration of the contract Tom was adjudged an idiot by the court, and Bethune was appointed his guardian at Tom's own request and that of his brothers and sisters. He is devoted to the family and does not want to go anywhere else. Besides all the liberty one could have under a business engagement, he is humored as a child in all the whims of a blind idiot, and has always had all the instruction he was capable of receiving."

David Marks has just been acquitted at Covington of a charge of theft in a trial characterized by a very remarkable coincidence. A few nights ago the smoke-house of Mr. Joseph Sockwell was raided, and quite an amount of meat was stolen. The buggy in which it was removed was tracked in the direction of Dave's house. Upon learning that he had a quantity of meat similar to that stolen, Mr. Sockwell obtained a search warrant and, accompanied by an officer, made a search of Mark's house, and a piece of what appeared to be shoulder meat with the blade bone in it was found. It had the imprint of a corncob, clearly defined, upon the skin part of it. On the trial of the case Mr. Sockwell swore that it was his practice to salt down his meat on cobs, and he was satisfied the piece in evidence was a part of that stolen from him. The defendant claimed that it was not shoulder meat, but a piece of "jole" bought by him from his landlord, William Adams. Mr. Adams testified that a few days before the search was instituted he had sold to Marks a "jole," and exhibited to the court one from his smokehouse, on which there appeared an imprint of a corncob. In the opinion of the court the guilt or innocence of the prisoner depended upon whether the piece of bone in the meat found in Dave's house was of the jaw or shoulder blade. Dr. J. A. Wright was called in as an expert, and used his knife in the dissection of both pieces and pronounced them similar, and as being parts of the "jole." The defendant was discharged.

John Kane and Kate Thurston, 19 and 18 years respectively, eloped from Rockford, Ills. Tuesday evening, and Anna Smith, daughter of a wealthy Pectatonica farmer, fled to Dakota with her father's hired man.

Saturday, August 1.

In a boat race at Detroit Thursday Hanlan easily defeated Lee.

Turkey has contracted for $3,500,000 worth o. new heavy artillery.

Dwight L. Moody has been seriously ill at Newport, and is by no means well yet.

The Kansas City Times suggests that Missouri and Kansas build a grand monument to Grant at Fort Leavenworth.

A fine black saddle-horse has been sent to Mr. Blaine by an admirer at Leavenworth, Kan. The horse is valued at $1,500.

League ball games Friday resulted: Chicago 9, Philadelphia 0; Detroit 3, Boston 2; New York 10, Buffalo 7; Providence 4, St. Louis 1.

Miss Blanche Williams, of Brantford, Ont., who has just matriculated in the University of Toronto, is the first colored girl ever admitted to the privileges of the university.

Extensive deposits of bituminous coal have been discovered in the vicinity of Lampasas, Tex.

A Dublin dispatch states that the registrar general's quarterly return estimates the present population of Ireland at 4,094,-342.

Extradition papers have been granted at Victoria, British Columbia, in the case of Hibbs, the defaulting postmaster of Lewiston, Idaho.

Twelve hundred coal miners in the Massillon, Ohio, district have stopped work in anticipation of a strike against a reduction of wages.

George W. Baker arrived at Boston Friday, having traveled from St. Louis, 1,354 miles, on his bicycle in nineteen days of actual riding.

In the National league base ball games Saturday the following were the scores: New York 7, Chicago 6; Providence 4. Detroit 1; Philadelphia 6, Buffalo 4.

In the office of the master in chancery in San Francisco Friday Judge David P. Terry, counsel for Miss Hill, attacked Sharon's attorney with his cane. Ex-Minister of France, the Hon. Levi P. Morton, with his family, arrived in New York Sunday.

Secretary Lamar and Attorney General Garland will remain in Washington during the president's absence. The other members of the cabinet will take a vacation.

LACK OF LAW IN LAURENS. AN INVESTIGATION OF THE RECENT OUTRAGES. A Negro Murdered by a Negro---A Suspicious Lynching--Public Opinion in Laurens C. H., Forces the Resignation of the Intendant and Wardens on Account of the Irby Case --- Milam more Scarrd than Hurt --- The Dastardly Assassination of Warren Bennett---What the People of Laurens Think about the Outrages --- The Inefficient Character of the Officers of the Law. THE NEWS AND COURTER BUREAU OAKLAND, CALIFORNIA JULY 20
On the 19th of July Alfred Dean, alias Alfred Harley, colored, shot and killed Mack Byrd, also colored. The next day Coroner Job J. Boozer held an inquest, the evidence taken being fled in the office of the Clerk of Court on July 28. The murderer had fled, but the Governor had not been notified of the result of the inquest or of the flight until the 30th of July. There was nothing remarkable about this case, and I did not investigate it further.

A Peculiar Lynching.

On the night of the Fourth of July Charles Williams, colored, who had been arrested for an alleged attempt to ravish a young white girl, was being conveyed under guard to Laurens Court House, when he was taken from the constables and shot to death in the public road, about five and a half miles from Laurens Court House. The inquest was held on the 5th inst. by Trial Justice W. B. Toddard, acting coroner, but the evidence was only filed with the Clerk of the Court on the 27th, and no report has been made to the Governor.

The evidence recorded is very brief and covers only the testimony of Constable J. A. Burdett, his assistant, Eddie Shell, and J. A. Rodgers, who found the dead body in the road. The evidence of the two first was to the effect that they were leading Williams by the rope with which he was bound; that he complained that he could hardly travel on account of the beating he had received that morning; that while he was going along and assseverating his innocence his conductors were halted by twelve or fifteen men, whose color they did not discern, although no mention of masks is recorded; that these men helped themselves to the prisoner, while he protested his innocence, and took him down the road, and that his late keepers heard shots fired and went on to Laurens. There is no mention of any resistance on the part of either guard or prisoner. Mr. Rodgers testified to finding the negro in the road shot through the head. An account of this lynching from one standpoint has already appeared in the News and Courier. The negro was stated to have been identified as one who entered the room on a young girl at night and placed his hand upon her head, but who, alarmed by her outcry, retreated precipitately. I have been informed of another side of the story. It is alleged by persons acquainted with the family that three elder sisters of the girl were of loose character, and surmised that the negro mistook her for one of them. The inference is a horrible one, but it belongs to the case and cannot be ignored.

Comment.—Lynching as a punishment for attempts upon female honor is an established and approved practice in South Carolina; but the scent evidence in this case and the soffo voice talk which one hears impress me with the opinion that there should be a more searching investigation of the facts.

The Irby Case.

The News and Courier has already published in full the Laurensville Herald's statement of both sides of the Irby matter, and it is unnecessary for me to repeat the details. It is admitted that Mr. Palmer and Col. J. L. M. Irby had words as to their relative muscle; that Col. Irby told Palmer that he declined to put himself on a level with him, but that he would furnish a man who would whip him; that he brought his negro servant, San Chapell, to town stood by with a pistol while the negro battered Palmer with his fists; that he admitted his violation of the town ordinance and expressed his willingness to be tried; that he heard that Mr. J. J. Pluss had spoken disparagingly of him, and got intoxicated on the strength of it; that he armed himself with a Winchester rifle and revolver, paraded the public square cursing and threatening his supposed enemies; that he sought Mr. Pluss and lunged at him with the muzzle of his rifle; that Mr. Pluss caught it and wrenched it from him and that he then drow his revolver and was disarmed of that also; that Mr. Pluss and Col. Irby's brother bore him to the ground and that Mr. Pluss choked him a little to subdue him, and held him down until he was taken to a carriage and conveyed to his home several miles from the town; that when sober he returned to town and readily gave two bonds for five hundred dollars each—one for assault with intent to kill and the other a peace bond—both being the result of warcouts sworn out by Mr. Pluss.

Col. Irby expressed a desire to see me and talked freely, moderately and courteously on the subject. He admitted, he said, that it was not lawful for him to knock people about, or to get a substitute to do it, but he thought that in the case of Palmer it was excusable on account of the character of the man. Palmer had made himself very obnoxious to gentlemen and was constantly embroiled. He had insulted him and dared a fight and he had selected a negro of about his size and put him to the test. His relations with Mr. Pluss had been very friendly and he had naught against him. He did not remember anything about his assault on him for he was intoxicated.

He did not admit, however, that he had in any degree sought to kill him. He desired to say that he condemned lawlessness as heartily as any man. He had himself broken the law, but he did not shirk the consequences.

"Whiskey," I suggested, "was at the bottom of the whole affair?"

"Yes" was the reply, "you are about right."

I interviewed Mr. Pluss, who is a member of a large mercantile firm, and has an excellent standing in the community. He said that Col. Irby when sober was entirely inoffensive and courteous, but when intoxicated was almost crazy. He had no feeling against him, but he had sworn out the warrants from a sense of public duty. It was a disgrace to the town that a man should be permitted to go armed about the streets, threatening and cursing and assaulting without hindrance by the authorities. He wisened the law vindicated and turbulence suppressed, once for all. He could have taken Col. Irby's own gun or pistol and killed him, but he declined to take advantage of what would have been his legal right. He intended only to bring him face to face with the law.

Mr. Palmer is not favorably regarded in Laurens. He is a Canadian, a painter by trade, and has been in the town only a few months. It is said in all quarters that he is frequently intoxicated, and that when so he is insolent to people who have said nothing to him and seeks quarrels and street fights.

Col. Irby is said to be a veritable madman when intoxicated, but at other times quiet and courteous. As to the action of the officials, Sheriff Ballew denied point blank that he was present when either assault occurred. He was the one who arrested Col. Irby at his home.

Mr. Charles Myers, the town marshal, (and the only local peace officer) is said to be a determined man. It is stated that he went to the acting intendant, Mr. F. Robertson, and asked him if he should arrest Col. Irby. The intendant was indifferent and said that he "night as well let the thing go!" At this reply the marshal pulled off his badge, put down his club and resigned. In view of the resignation of the intendant and council he was afterwards induced to serve until a new council should be elected. It is believed that he would have made the arrest promptly if authorized to do so.

The people of the town whom I talked to criticised the management of the affair very freely. Considering

On Tuesday morning the people of Laurens Courthouse were still uninformed as to the affair. It was not even known in the office of the clerk of Court whether the Inquest had been concluded, as no papers had been filed there.

Having obtained from Col. Crews the names of some of the best-informed and most-reliable citizens of that section who could be depended upon for information, I took a buggy on Tuesday morning and spent the day in gathering information, driving thirty miles for the purpose. The gentlemen to whom I applied impressed me as honorable, fair-minded men, and they spoke freely, with the request, however, that their names should not be used. This caution, I think, is justifiable in a neighborhood where three men have within six years been assassinated while at work in their fields.

Warren Bennett was a negro youth of about sixteen years of age. He had a crippled sister, according to common report. The stepfather of the two, Steve Sullivan, last spring caught Wade Bolt, a young white man, nineteen years old, in criminal intercourse with his step-daughter. Bolt tried to bribe him to keep the matter quiet, but it got out and Bolt's comrades jeered at him for his connection with the crippled girl. Warren Bennett heard of it and had a controversy with Bolt about it. They had a scuffle on the subject. According to the same report and belief, Lucas Aberronable, John Griffin and Joe Avery, young white men, on one occasion, called to visit young Bolt's sisters and were snubbed by them. Seeking revenge and knowing that Bolt and the negro were on bad terms they went to Bennett and tried to bribe him to say that for twenty-five cents any one could do what he pleased with the Bolt girls. The negro peremptorily refused. The young men then, rather than give up their project, themselves circulated the report that Bennett had made the statement they wished him to make. This was admitted after the shooting by a boy who heard the proposals to Bennett, and it proved that he was guiltless of wrong. The report circulated, as all such reports do. This was in June. On Thursday, the 9th of July, as Bennett was boeing cotton on Mr. J. E. Tumblin's place at the Hickory Tavern Crossroads he was assassinated. The hour was about 7 o'clock in the morning. In the evening Trial Justice Joel Ellison, who lives at
Tumblin's place at the Hickory Tavern Crossroads he was assassinated. The hour was about 7 o'clock in the morning. In the evening Trial Justice Joel Ellison, who lives at Triangle, five or six miles away, went to Hickory Tavern, and, acting as coroner, began the inquest. On Saturday evening the inquest was concluded by a verdict that Warren Bennett had come to his death at the hands of some person or persons to the jury unknown. I was told that Trial Justice Ellison is related to or closely connected with Bolt's family. This, however, was questioned by other persons. I was told also that eight members of the coroner's jury were relatives or connections of Bolt. A gentleman who challenged this, however, counted up four members of the jury who were—John Armstrong, Pleas, Bolt, Stobo Bolt and Neil Knight—but said that several would have been impartial no matter what relationship existed.

As Trial Justice Ellison lived too far off for me to visit him I had no opportunity of seeing the evidence taken at the inquest, as he had not filed it. I heard from gentlemen who were present some of the testimony, but it was mixed with other facts not testified to but believed, that I cannot distinguish between them. This, however, is what was given me as information entitled to credit, and embraces what was put in evidence and what was not:

Before the killing, Bolt's mother told Bennett's mother that her son had better get away or he would be killed. On the day of the assassination there was to be a Sunday-school celebration at Mount Bethel church, some five miles from Hickory Tavern. Mr. Clark, who lives near the tavern, says that that morning Wade Bolt came to his house and inquired for Epps Hellams, a young white man and his uncle. He wanted to know if he had passed. Hearing that he had not Bolt went on. He was dressed in black and had a black slouch hat. He took the direction of Hickory Tavern. The place where the shooting occurred is on the road between Mr. Clark's and Mr. Tumblin's house at the Tavern crossroads. A strip of wood—the only one about—runs along the fence where the first shot was fired. The houses named were about four hundred yards apart. A few minutes after Bolt left Mr. Clark heard two or three shots in the direction of the place where Bennett was killed. Mrs. Tumblin and a little girl were working in the field about seventy-five yards from Bennett, who was apoint ten steps from the fence. Mrs. Tumblin testified at the inquest that she heard the first shot and saw Bennett fall. Then she turned her
five yards from Bennett, who was about ten steps from the fence. Mrs. Tumbilin testified at the inquest that she heard the first shot and saw Bennett fall. Then she turned her head away and when she looked again a man dressed in black, with a black hat slouched over his eyes, ran from the cover of the fence to where the negro was lying and shot him again as he lay on the ground. He then ran off. She testified that she did not recognize the man, but took him for a white man by the color of his hands. The little girl gave similar testimony.

In private Mrs. Tumbilin is said to have asserted that Bolt was the murderer, but she did not so testify. Soon after the shooting Bolt is said to have appeared at a house a few hundred yards away, which he could only have reached without the notice of people in the fields around—and they noticed nobody—by passing along the strip of timber from which the shot was fired. He was flushed and had his collar and necktie in his hand as if he had been running. He made his way to the Hellams's house in the rear of Clark's. After awhile he and Epps Hellams drove by Clark's house toward the Tavern crossroads in the direction Bolt had taken previously, and went on to the Sunday-school celebration.

In the evening Hellams returned from the celebration and attended the inquest, but Bolt was not with him. A constable who went to arrest Bolt subsequently said that he ascertained that on the morning of the murder Hellams loaned the pistol to Bolt with five chambers loaded, and that at 3 o'clock on the day after Bolt returned it with only three chambers loaded. Hellams was said to have asserted that he had in his pocket the pistol that had done the shooting, but that he had not used it himself.

Dr. J. S. Wolf made the post-mortem examination and testified at the inquest that one ball had entered the body just in front of the left shoulder, passing into the chest between the third and fourth ribs and through both lungs and lodged in the front portion of the right shoulder-brace, embedding itself in the bone. The other ball entered the back of the head and came out to the left of the left eye. It was thought that the balls came from a 36 or 38 calibre pistol.

I was told that Bolt appeared at the inquest on Saturday armed with a big stick and that Hellams was there with a double-barrelled shotgun. Trial Justice Ellison took no action after the inquest until Monday, when Steve Sulivan, the stepfather of the murdered boy, swore out a warrant for Bolt. The warrant was not dispatched until Tuesday, when it was not strange that Bolt was not found at home. No hunt was made for him. Lawlessness in Laurens. [News and (survey]
The special correspondent of the News and Courier who was sent to Laurens County a few days ago to investigate the several instances of lawlessness which have recently occurred in that county has performed the duty assigned to him, and reports, the result in a letter which we published to-day.

The inquiries of our correspondent were conducted in a careful and impartial spirit, with no other purpose than to elicit the truth, and as the information which he obtained was derived from the most trustworthy sources, there can be no question as to its substantial accuracy. It shows, moreover, that the accounts of the lawlessness in Laurens County which have already been published in the News and Courier and in the Laurensville Herald have not exaggerated either the nature of the crimes or the indifference and neglect displayed by the local authorities in failing to discharge their duty with reference to the criminals.

It is not necessary to repeat the details that have been given in regard to the assaults instigated and committed by Col. Irby upon Palmer and Pluss, respectively. There were numerous witnesses of these assaults, and both will be made the subject of a judicial investigation, the results of which may not properly be anticipated. Col. Irby is under bond to answer to the serious charges made against him, and the people of Laurens must now look to their Courts to assert and vindicate the law which he admits that he has violated. It is stated that Col. Irby is a courteous gentleman and good citizen when not under the influence of liquor, and no one should know better than himself the gravity of his offence and the necessity for its punishment. When men of his character and standing give way to violent passion and imperil the lives of their fellow-men with impunity, under whatever circumstances, it is not surprising that their example should be followed by men of lower class, who are without the restraining influence of education, personal pride and social position, and that lawlessness should prevail among them to any extent.

There is nothing to be said save in the way of strong condemnation in regard to the lynching of the negro Charles Williams, and the deliberate and hastily murder of the colored boy Warren Bennett. In the case of Williams the victim was taken from the custody of the officers of the law while carnestly protesting his innocence, and was shot dead in the public highway by the self-appointed jury and executioners. There is no hint that even a form of irregular trial was had in this case and the victim was apparently sacrifice.
in the public highway by the self-appointed jury and executioners. There is no hint that even a form of irregular trial was had in this case, and the victim was apparently sacrificed to the blind rage of his murderers, without an effort on their part to established the fact of his guilt.

In the other case, that of the killing of Bennett, the testimony so far obtained shows that the murder was one of the most atrocious crimes ever committed in this State. It should have been promptly investigated, and the delay that has already occurred in its investigation casts a deep reproach upon the responsible officials of the county. The testimony of a number of persons points clearly to one or both of two men as being concerned in the murder; their names and the circumstances which indicate their guilt are generally known and discussed in the county, but no effort was made to arrest them until sufficient time had elapsed to allow them to escape.

The story of the alleged ill treatment of the emigration agent, Milam, which was first published in an Atlanta paper, appears to have been greatly exaggerated. The truth in regard to this occurrence is, apparently, that Milam became frightened in view of the threatening demonstrations made against him and fled the county without waiting for hostilities to begin. The pistol salute which hastened his sudden departure will suggest to many persons, however, that Milam did not leave too soon for his own comfort and safety.

Our correspondent was assured, and found reason to believe, that public sentiment in Laurens County is strongly opposed to the condition of affairs which provails there, and that the law abiding people of the county appreciate the injury that must result to them if the impression obtains abroad that the county is not a safe place to live in. It is very significant, however, that the colored people of the county have so far adsorbed that impression that large numbers of them have already moved away, and that it is necessary to banish emigration agents at the point of the pistol. It is time for the law-abiding citizens to declare and enforce their sentiments when colored laborers are afraid to work in the fields alone, and when white men are afraid to testify to crimes of which they have knowledge.

In view of the facts which are presented in the letter of our correspondent it will scarcely be disputed that a state of things exists in Laurens County that should be speedily remedied. The crimes enumerated are assuredly of a character to demand the promptest and most determined action on the part of the officers of the law, but such action has

Even the plainest and simplest requirements of the criminal statutes have been disregarded, and official reports of brutal murders have been pigcon-hoiled for weeks, instead of being forwarded to the State authorities for the attention they required, and which was necessary to promote the ends of justice.

The people of Laurens County are said to be fully alive to the evils described and to the necessity of a change for the better. This is well, but it is not enough. Mere sentiment will accomplish nothing unless it is expressed and enforced. The root of the trouble manifestly lies in the inefficiency of the local authorities, and the work of reform must begin with them. The people of the county owe it to themselves and to the State to turn out the men who misrepresent them in public office, and who hold so lax views of their duties. A great deal has been accomplished in fixing the blame where it belongs, and the citizens of Laurens and Governor Thompson will not fail to do the rest.

Coming East For Money.
It is said that both parties to the state campaign in Ohio are short of funds. No patriot need grieve over this state of things, for it means less corruption and a curtailment of the wanton use of money in politics; but the article which conveys the above facts goes on to say that both the democratic and republican parties are coming East to beg for funds. Now this statement, if reliable, reveals a nice state of things. We hear a vast deal about the time of the national conventions concerning the mighty West as the seat of power and wealth, and reservoir of great and patriotic men; but it seems that the politicians of the Buckeye state feel that it is necessary for them to come East for money with which to run their local campaign. Did you ever hear of Massachusetts or New York asking the men of Cincinnati, Cleveland or Chicago to contribute money toward the conduct of a purely state fight? Not much. The West brags in a very breezy and captivating way, but the fact is that people out there have become so used to running East on begging expenditures for colleges, schools and churches.

Who 'have been faithless to their trusts?' ask these papers. But the interrogations do not cover the ground. No fact is plainer in American politics than that there is a new taste in the South for men of better mettle; and this taste has been created by a recognition of the principles that determine the main body of Grover Cleveland's appointments. The change is marked, sudden, unexpected and radical. The southern commonwealths have had their emancipations from carpet-bag governments for six or eight years, but it has been only within six months that they have thought of politics broader than faction or deeper than caucus convictions. The "new 'South' of the magazine writers and stump-speakers was an industrial new South up to this year. Otherwise, what occasion should there be for the Charleston News and Courier to record this political fact: "The state was 'redeemed in 1876. Is it not time that the 'minor offices be reformed?' The minor offices in the mind of the writer were those of the trial justices of South Carolina. It is quite likely that the News had in mind the letter of Trial Justice Ellerson, published a few weeks ago in defense of his official course in one of the murder cases in the now notorious Laurens county. Here is a choice specimen of that letter:

Now whare is the consistancy in centuring me for not isureing a warrant on the verdic. On a Monday fallowing Steve Sullivan the step father of Warren Bennett came to my office and swore out a warrant on Information and bilief for the arrest of Wade W Bolt for the murder of Warren Bennett. Said warrant was granted and put into of a duly artherized constable who precedid as soon as poserable to make the arrest and failed to find Wade Bolt. After which several surches was made for Wade Bolt and failed to find him I then place the warrant in the hands of the surriffe and He has made a surch with like results It has alco been alledge that myself and the Bolt family were closely connected by tyes of relation ship which acquisition is false as no degree of relationship exist between me and the Bolt family.

The Laurensville Herald has since expressed the opinion that if Gov Thompson shall undertake to reduce to the ranks every trial justice who is deficient in spelling, "the state would 'soon be minus a large number holding 'these positions.' The News and Courier holds that "were the choice necessarily between an honest fellow and an irreproachable speller, the man of high personal character would, and should, be taken despite his defective orthography." But the important thing is that these papers do not admit the necessity of such an alternative, but they do record the growing demand for better men. This low quality of men is not a new thing, but the demand for a "new deal" is encouraging. The very first papers of the state admit that the standard of the justices is scandalously low in South Carolina. The bringing of these justices to the front at this time is caused by the epidemic of unpunished murders in that state. Charleston itself has a trial justice who last week discharged two men in the face of the most convincing testimony of murderous guilt, and this justice knew how to spell too. The prospect is that Trial Justice Williman dug his political grave when he let these men go, and the politics of the city, if not the state, may turn upon this very court drama. The temper of the Charleston public must be indeed disturbed when crime and politics can be discussed in one breath from the pulpit, as it was on Sunday last by Rev W. H. Lawrence, who said among other things:—

Perhaps also I should not allude to the fact that the city government is divided into two wings, one the liberal party and the other the hourbon party, that in years gone by cried down the negro as a beast. Strange it is that the political differences of local parties should be a cause of delay and obstruction in the performance of a duty as far as the investigation of this murder is concerned. That is one of the chief difficulties. We have one of the parties offering a reward and linking themselves for that purpose with the thinking and representative colored men of this city, and the other party which says openly, "Here you are and no further shall you go." Of the two parties, let me advise you to ally yourselves with the liberals. You may look to the end of time and never again will you see the old republican party rise up and regain the mastery and control of this city or state. But far be it from me to counsel you to disregard the operations of the law, or to take that law in your own hands. It is for you to act as if you believed that if the murderer was found to be a white man he will be punished as the law prescribes.
